item.description: YAT Sen Secondary School will look to continue its strong netball progress when the Central Rally gets underway today. The school has built a growing presence in the sport, with its players developing through a program that blends basketball skills with netball training.
item.content:encoded:
YAT Sen Secondary School will look to continue its strong netball progress when the Central Rally gets underway today.

The school has built a growing presence in the sport, with its players developing through a program that blends basketball skills with netball training.

Coach Sikeli Tuwai says the transition has helped keep players fit while improving their understanding of the game.

Yat Sen’s Under-19 Open Boys side also enters the competition as three-time national champions, although this year’s squad faces the challenge of rebuilding after losing several experienced players.

The school will now aim to turn its preparation into another strong Central Rally campaign.

item.title: Split over rule | Guest player move under scrutiny
item.description: THE Fiji Secondary Schools Rugby Union’s (FSSRU) decision to allow qualified schools to register up to six guest players for the Vodafone Deans U18 elimination and quarterfinal stages has received mixed reactions from schools in the Western and Eastern zones. While some schools have welcomed the move, saying it will give smaller schools a better chance of competing at the national level, Queen Vic
item.content:encoded:
THE Fiji Secondary Schools Rugby Union’s (FSSRU) decision to allow qualified schools to register up to six guest players for the Vodafone Deans U18 elimination and quarterfinal stages has received mixed reactions from schools in the Western and Eastern zones.

While some schools have welcomed the move, saying it will give smaller schools a better chance of competing at the national level, Queen Victoria School principal Epeli Nasau believes the new format requires greater consultation with school heads.

Under the updated rules, schools that qualify for the national eliminations and quarterfinals can bring in up to six guest players — three forwards and three backs from schools that have been eliminated within the same zone.

Ba Methodist School coach David Wise welcomed the decision, saying it could help smaller schools strengthen their squads and give more students the opportunity to experience Deans rugby.

“We are so happy about this news. This is good news for us, and it will benefit smaller schools,” Wise said.

He said Ba Methodist had already benefited from the opportunity, with players joining their lower-grade teams from other schools.

“Our Ba Methodist U15 side, we have brought in a few players from Xavier, and their parents are happy that their children are playing in the Deans competition, which is always their dream from primary school,” Wise said.

Wise said the rule had also helped address a shortage in their U17 side.

“Our Ba Methodist U17 team, we are getting one tight head from Natabua. We only have one tight head prop, so we are getting one from Natabua. This is the benefit of getting guest players in the team,” he said.

“We are excited about this new rule, and we look forward to a tough quarterfinal.”

However, Nasau believes the new system should have been discussed with school heads before its introduction.

The FSSRU has introduced a 16-team elimination round, changing the pathway teams follow after completing their respective zone competitions.

“To be honest, from my side, it should be a consultation. If you can sit together with FSSRU and heads of school, then we discuss,” Nasau said.

He said consultation would have allowed schools to consider the financial and wider implications of the new format, including player movement between schools and the impact on families.

Nasau also questioned the fairness of allowing players to join another school during the competition, particularly for teams that have gone through the entire season with their own players.

“For those who have been in the journey from day one up until the elimination stage, it’s going to be a little bit unfair,” he said.

He said school rugby was built around commitment, attendance, parental support, attitude and character, with players developing a strong connection with the school they represent.

“We bleed for our school. We bleed for the name of the school for years,” Nasau said.

Another concern raised by Nasau is the reduced preparation and recovery time before the national quarterfinals.

He said teams traditionally had a week to recover and prepare after completing their zone competition, but the new format leaves little time for teams to regroup.

The additional travel required under the new system could also increase costs for schools and disrupt academic programs and classroom learning, he said.

Despite his concerns, Nasau said schools must now accept the decision and make the most of the new system.

“The ball is in our court now. The only thing we are going to do, let’s welcome the system,” he said.

Nasau believes the first year should be used as an opportunity to assess the new format, including its costs and benefits, before schools provide feedback on how the system could be improved in future.

The U18 elimination round will be played this Saturday, with the quarterfinals scheduled for the following weekend.

item.title: Rugby growth inspires youth
item.description: RUGBY Australia’s general manager of Women’s Rugby, Jilly Collins, believes the continued growth of Super Rugby Women’s is inspiring more young girls across Fiji and Australia to take up the sport. Collins said the competition provides the region’s best female players with a platform to showcase their talent while creating role models for future generations.
item.content:encoded:
RUGBY Australia’s general manager of Women’s Rugby, Jilly Collins, believes the continued growth of Super Rugby Women’s is inspiring more young girls across Fiji and Australia to take up the sport.

Collins said the competition provides the region’s best female players with a platform to showcase their talent while creating role models for future generations.

“What Super Rugby Women’s does is puts the best rugby players on the platform across Australia and Fiji,” Collins said.

“There’s so much pride behind these players and teams. It really does inspire the next generation of players that can look at their heroes and say, ‘I want to give that a go too.’”

She said increasing participation among young girls remains one of Rugby Australia’s biggest goals.

“Seeing participation numbers in both Fiji and Australia increasing is what it’s all about at the end of the day.”

“As much as it’s a wonderful spectacle, giving more opportunities for girls to play rugby is the silver lining in everything.”

Following next week’s champions clash between the NSW Waratahs and the winners of New Zealand’s Super Rugby Aupiki competition, Collins said attention would quickly turn to the international calendar.

She noted that the Fijiana will host South Africa in Fiji, while the Wallaroos will cross the Tasman to face the Black Ferns in Auckland.

Looking ahead to the 2027 Super Rugby Women’s season, Collins said planning would begin almost immediately after the current campaign concludes.

“We’ll give ourselves about a week break and then we start planning for 2027 to make it a bigger, better and more competitive competition than ever,” she said.

Collins said the long-term vision is to continue strengthening the competition while creating more opportunities for women and girls to play rugby throughout the region.

item.title: U18 team chases history in Romania
item.description: THE Fiji Women’s Under-18 handball team’s historic trip to the international Women’s Federation Championship in Romania later this month is about more than simply competing against the world’s best. For head of delegation Lusi Rokoura, the campaign represents the beginning of a new era for handball in Fiji.
item.content:encoded:
THE Fiji Women’s Under-18 handball team’s historic trip to the international Women’s Federation Championship in Romania later this month is about more than simply competing against the world’s best.

For head of delegation Lusi Rokoura, the campaign represents the beginning of a new era for handball in Fiji.

The 12-member squad will make history as the first Pacific Island nation to compete at the IHF Women’s Youth World Championship after qualifying through the IHF Trophy Oceania Championship in the Cook Islands last October.

While the immediate focus remains on facing world powers France, Croatia and Egypt, Rokoura believes the long-term impact of the tournament could help transform the sport locally.

“We hope to come back and do more awareness trainings in the Western Division, Eastern, Northern and also enter into schools competitions,” Rokoura said.

She expects the tournament to bring invaluable experience for the young squad, who are all still in school, while also creating awareness and strengthening the growth of handball locally.

Rokoura said the growth of the sport would continue beyond World Championship, with plans to strengthen the women’s pathway and create more opportunities for players at national and grassroots level.

“Our national women’s team are currently training for that. Our youth pathway, they will come back and regroup with them.”

Officials hope to strengthen development pathways by expanding handball programs across schools and communities, giving more young athletes the opportunity to take up the sport.

For Rokoura, the vision extends even further.

“It’s exciting to for us as we build up to the 2032 Summer Olympic Games.”

While results in Romania will be important, the bigger victory may lie in the legacy this team leaves behind.

As Fiji prepares to make history on the world stage, the U18 side is not only carrying the nation’s hopes but also helping pave the way for future generations of players.

Their journey could ultimately be the turning point, inspiring a new wave of participation and laying the foundations for the future of handball in Fiji.

item.title: MGM out to turn the table at eliminations
item.description: MAHATMA Gandhi Memorial School’s (MGM) Weet-Bix Raluve U18 side is determined to make the most of its second chance after securing a place in the Vodafone Deans national elimination rounds despite finishing runners-up in the Southern Zone competition. MGM went down 0-18 to Lomary Secondary School in Saturday’s Southern Zone final, but coach Antonio Rabulika believes the experience has prepared his
item.content:encoded:
MAHATMA Gandhi Memorial School’s (MGM) Weet-Bix Raluve U18 side is determined to make the most of its second chance after securing a place in the Vodafone Deans national elimination rounds despite finishing runners-up in the Southern Zone competition.

MGM went down 0-18 to Lomary Secondary School in Saturday’s Southern Zone final, but coach Antonio Rabulika believes the experience has prepared his young side for the bigger challenge ahead.

“We came to win, but then we didn’t play our cards right,” Rabulika said.

“Most of our players are playing for the first time in the grand final. We know very well that the Lomary team is full of very good players.

“We tried as much as we could not to play according to their game, but it’s the first time we’re playing in the final, so we’re satisfied with what we did.”

Rather than dwelling on the result, Rabulika said the team’s focus had shifted to the national elimination rounds, where MGM would represent the Southern Zone as runners-up.

“We’re going to the national quarters as runners-up from the South. We have another week to reset and then we’ll reload again.

“And we’ll see what the results are. Hopefully our next one will be better than what we had today.”

The coach said one of the team’s priorities would be improving its ability to control possession after being denied opportunities in the final.

“Today we were denied a lot of possession. That is one area that we have to work on. Without the ball, we really can’t score any points.”

Despite the setback, Rabulika believes the Southern Zone competition has been an important stepping stone for the players, many of whom were experiencing a final for the first time.

“I think it’s a really good competition. Whoever performs at this stage will rise to the top, whether it’s in the Rooster Chicken Fijian Drua Women or the Fijiana program.”

With another opportunity still ahead, MGM will now look to regroup, learn from Saturday’s experience and approach the national elimination rounds with renewed confidence.

item.title: Fijian Drua W reward players
item.description: THE McDonald’s Fijian Drua Women capped off another memorable campaign by celebrating their achievements at the club’s annual presentation night at the Sofitel Fiji Resort and Spa on Tuesday night. The awards night brought together players, coaches, sponsors, partners, families and supporters to reflect on an outstanding 2026 Super Rugby Women’s campaign.
item.content:encoded:
THE McDonald’s Fijian Drua Women capped off another memorable campaign by celebrating their achievements at the club’s annual presentation night at the Sofitel Fiji Resort and Spa on Tuesday night.

The awards night brought together players, coaches, sponsors, partners, families and supporters to reflect on an outstanding 2026 Super Rugby Women’s campaign.

The Drua women have now reached four Super Rugby Women’s grand finals in five years and this season added another milestone by claiming the minor premiership for only the second time. Their top-of-the-table finish also earned Fiji the right to host its first Super Rugby Women’s grand final, marking another historic moment for women’s rugby in the country.

Six major awards were presented during the evening, recognising excellence both on and off the field.

Josivini Naihamu emerged as the biggest winner of the night, claiming both the Encore Players’ Player of the Year and the prestigious McDonald’s Fiji Player of the Year awards.

Ruth Raketekete received the Punjas Community Champion Award after unanimously being recognised by the club staff for her outstanding service away from the rugby field.

Youngest player in the squad Carletta Yee was named the Mogul Fan Player of the Year after becoming one of the competition’s most popular players through her impressive performances and strong connection with supporters.

The Rooster Chicken Women’s Rookie of the Year Award went to Varanisese Qoro, whose outstanding debut Super Rugby Women’s season earned widespread praise for her professionalism, discipline and rapid development.

The Fiji Airways Try of the Year was decided by live voting during the presentation night from a shortlist featuring tries by Aqela Raitubu, Naihamu and Kolora Lomani providing a fitting finale to a night celebrating another landmark chapter in the Drua Women’s remarkable journey. Naihamu was awarded the Try of the Year adding to her third awards of the season.

McDonald’s Fiji Fijian Drua Women’s player Carletta Yee (left) receives the 2026 Mogul Fan Player of the Year award from Mogul Pte Ltd director Monisha Naidu during the McDonald’s Fiji Fijian Drua Women’s team awards night held at the Sofitel Fiji Resort and Spa in Denarau Nadi on 28th July 2026. item.title: Savusavu sailors chase national honours
item.description: YOUNG sailors from Savusavu are seeking support to travel to Suva for the national championships, with the opportunity carrying significance beyond the competition itself. For these athletes, sailing has become a pathway to discipline, confidence and purpose, while keeping them involved in a positive activity and away from the streets.
item.content:encoded:
YOUNG sailors from Savusavu are seeking support to travel to Suva for the national championships, with the opportunity carrying significance beyond the competition itself.

For these athletes, sailing has become a pathway to discipline, confidence and purpose, while keeping them involved in a positive activity and away from the streets.

The sport has also opened opportunities for young sailors to travel overseas, experience different cultures and represent Fiji internationally.

Savusavu has established itself as an important centre for sailing in Fiji, with the town producing several sailors who have gone on to represent the country on the international stage.

That record has given the youths of Savusavu something to aspire to while strengthening the community’s connection with the sport.

For the young sailors, every training session and competition provides an opportunity to develop skills that extend beyond the water.

Sailing demands commitment, discipline, teamwork and confidence, qualities that can help shape young people as they grow.

Their involvement has also become a source of pride for the Savusavu community, with their achievements providing inspiration for younger athletes who may want to follow the same pathway.

However, competing at national level comes with challenges for athletes based outside Suva.

Travel and participation costs can create an added hurdle for young sailors from the North, making support important if they are to take part in major competitions.

The upcoming national championships in Suva would give the Savusavu sailors the opportunity to compete against some of the country’s best and gain valuable experience at a higher level.

It would also allow them to showcase the talent that continues to emerge from the town and strengthen their pathway towards future opportunities.

For Savusavu’s young sailors, reaching the nationals is therefore about more than winning races.

It is about giving them the chance to build confidence, gain experience and continue pursuing a sport that has already given them hope, purpose and a sense of belonging.

With Fiji surrounded by the ocean, the sailors believe the country has the natural environment to develop more athletes capable of competing on the international stage.

For this group from Savusavu, the immediate goal is to get to Suva, compete and make the most of an opportunity that could help shape their future in sailing.

item.title: Grammar eyes clean sweep
item.description: SUVA Grammar School is setting its sights on a clean sweep at the Central Rally, with coach Georgina Batisaresare challenging her players to build on a strong Southern Zone campaign. “Our aim is to try and win all four grades that we go in,” Batisaresare said
item.content:encoded:
SUVA Grammar School is setting its sights on a clean sweep at the Central Rally, with coach Georgina Batisaresare challenging her players to build on a strong Southern Zone campaign.

“Our aim is to try and win all four grades that we go in,” Batisaresare said

The Central Rally starts today at 3pm, with Friday set aside for a full day of competition as Grammar looks to carry its recent form into another demanding tournament.

Grammar enters the rally with confidence after producing a strong campaign at last Thursday’s Southern Zone 2 Secondary Schools Netball Finals.

The school captured the U15 and U19 titles, while also finishing runners-up in the U14 and Open Boys grades.

The U15 side defeated Saint Joseph’s Secondary School 22-10 before the U19 team secured the prestigious Vosarogo Trophy with a convincing 19-5 victory over the same opponent.

Grammar came close to claiming a third title in the U14 grade, narrowly losing 17-16 to Saint Joseph’s in one of the closest finals of the day.

Its Open Boys side also pushed for honours before going down 12-14 to Yat Sen Secondary School.

The results across the grades have given Grammar an encouraging platform heading into the Central Rally, with the school now looking to turn that consistency into further success.

Batisaresare was pleased with the effort from her players, saying the performances reflected the commitment shown throughout their preparation.

“I am very happy that all the teams we came with to play in the finals.

“We won the U15 grade and the U19 grade, but we are second in the U14 and Open Boys grade, and that is an achievement.”

The Central Rally will provide Grammar with another opportunity to test its depth across the four grades while identifying areas that need improvement.

Batisaresare said the immediate focus would be on improving fitness and refining the school’s style of play as the teams continue to develop.

The rally will also form part of Grammar’s wider preparation for the National Secondary Schools Netball Championships later this year.

After showing its strength across several grades at the Southern Zone finals, Grammar will now look to make the most of the Central Rally and continue building towards its national campaign.
